tldr: Let \(Q\) be a full-data law for \(X,A,Y^0,Y^1\) satisfying consistency and conditional exchangeability, and let \(P\) be its induced observed law for \(X,A,Y\). The continuous extension \(\tau_P(x_0)\) is an observed-law functional despite \(P(X=x_0)=0\). On the headline class with \(f_P(x)=|x-x_0|v_P(x)\), measurable \(2\le v_P\le6\), Hölder \(1/10\) propensity and baseline regression, and Lipschitz treatment effect, the sharp absolute-risk rate is \(n^{-1/5}\). A finite close-pair ratio attains the upper bound without estimating a nuisance or density, and an adjacent-overlap Bernoulli mixture under \(4|x-x_0|\) gives the matching all-estimator lower bound. More generally, the full measurable-envelope phase diagram is solved: the exponent is \(\min\{r_0,r_1\}\), and unknown observational nuisances slow the oracle exponent exactly when \(s<\gamma/(4\gamma+2)\). With known propensity, the matched rate is \(n^{-\gamma/(2\gamma+\kappa+1)}\); its \(\kappa=1,\gamma=1\) specialization is \(n^{-1/4}\), isolating the cost of rough confounding in the headline \(n^{-1/5}\) result.
gap: KennedyBalakrishnanRobinsWasserman2024 explicitly leaves the covariate-density role unresolved; its matched submodel uses different local support geometry. Gaiffas2005 gives degenerate-design regression rates without an unknown treatment mechanism, and GaoHan2020 studies integrated heterogeneous-effect loss. No located theorem gives both a finite density-free upper estimator and an all-estimator lower bound on the identical full-support linear-zero observational class.
fill: The project first defines the causal model as a full-data law \(Q\), its induced observed experiment \(P\), and the continuous-extension target as an observed-law functional. It then derives an exact pair-moment identity, a total close-pair ratio with uniform risk \(h+b^{1/5}+(nh^2)^{-1/2}+(n^2h^3b)^{-1/2}\), and a full-support randomized nuisance mixture with pointwise binary-cell cancellation and chi-square cost of order \(\exp(Cn^2a^4h^3b)-1\). The choices \(h=n^{-1/5}\), \(b=h^5\), and \(a^2\asymp h\) match the bounds.
